name: World Central Kitchen: emergency meals (charityevals)
summary: World Central Kitchen cooks and delivers hot meals after disasters and in wars; in 2025 it spent 372.5 million dollars on this, its only programme, and served 130 to 179 million meals, about 70% of them in Gaza, the rest mostly in Haiti, Ukraine, Jamaica, Myanmar and US and European disasters. The model values the meals as food on the site's log-income scale and, in Gaza and poorer countries' crises, as a share of the excess deaths from hunger they avert, in three branches split by the Form 990's regions: about 0.10 years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars at the defaults, over 70% of it from Gaza. Each branch's food is valued from its share of the food bill, over the months people were fed. The biggest uncertainties are how much of the food in Gaza others would have brought in through the same crossings, and how little people there had without it; no study measures what the meals do, so every branch is discounted for missing data.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

The Form 990 names Italy and Spain among the year's responses, and the Spanish affiliate also supports neighbouring responses; Ukraine's supply lines run through Poland and Romania. No split is published: about a quarter, from 5% to 50%. The rest counts with the rich-country disasters.

Meals served in 2025

source.title: World Central Kitchen, Inc. and Affiliate: consolidated financial statements, December 31, 2025 and 2024 (Grant Thornton, audited)
source.page: p. 11, note 1
source.quote: WCK served more than 179 plus million meals to families in 31 countries in 2025.

rows.explainer: The audited accounts say more than 179 million meals in 31 countries; the Form 990 and the charity's 2025 review say more than 130 million. The larger figure fits the Gaza counts below (about 130 million there alone), so it is the best guess, and 130 million the low end. The charity's own count; nobody checks it independently.

rows.label: Share of the year's meals served in Gaza

source.title: World Central Kitchen: 'One million hot meals a day in Gaza' (11 February 2026)
source.quote: over 272 million meals

rows.explainer: From the charity's dated Gaza counts: 70 million meals by October 2024 (its Middle East timeline), 122 million in Gaza and the West Bank by 3 March 2025, and 272 million by 11 February 2026, when it served a million meals a day (two series: the release's body says over 220 million hot meals, its footer and the milestone page 272 million meals, with 73 million loaves of bread counted apart). Taking out about 40 million in early 2026 and the 20 million or so of January and February 2025 leaves roughly 110 to 140 million meals in Gaza in 2025 on the 272 million series, about 70% of 179 million; on the hot-meal series about 85 million, 47%. About 70%, from 45% to 82%. It sets how long each person was fed, not the food's value, which comes from the branch's spending.

rows.label: Cost per meal in rich countries over poorer ones
rows.explainer: Meals in the US and Spain are bought from restaurants and food trucks at local wages and prices; in Haiti, Ukraine or Myanmar they are cooked in field kitchens with local staff. About 2.5 times, from 1.5 to 4 (US food prices and wages are several times Haiti's or Ukraine's, partly offset by more volunteers). It splits the meals outside Gaza between the two branches by their spending.

rows.label: Meals served in Gaza in 2025
Gaza: bread handed out in 2025, in meal-equivalents

source.title: World Central Kitchen: 'Gaza milestone' (11 February 2026)
source.quote: 73 million loaves of bread

rows.explainer: The charity's mobile bakeries gave out 73 million loaves in Gaza by February 2026 (counted apart from the meals; the flour is in the food bill), perhaps 30 to 40 million of them in 2025. Bread spreads the food over more days: at about half a meal's food per loaf, about 15 million meal-equivalents, from 5 to 30 million.

People in Gaza who got the charity's meals during 2025

source.title: World Central Kitchen: 'Gaza milestone' (11 February 2026)
source.quote: close to half of the total population

rows.explainer: Unique people over the year. In February 2026, at a million meals a day, the charity said close to half of Gaza's population (about 2.1 million) could rely on one of its meals each day; in most of 2025 it served fewer a day, but over the year people moved and the kitchens changed. About a million, from 600,000 to 1.5 million. Reach in the other branches is their meals over meals per person.

rows.label: Cost per person reached in Gaza
rows.explainer: Context: the Gaza branch's cost, overhead included, per person fed during the year.

rows.label: Meals a person gets from the charity on a day they are served
rows.explainer: Most sites hand out one hot meal per person a day (in Gaza a lunch-time hot meal; bread is counted separately in the charity's figures); some US and Caribbean responses serve two. About 1.2, from 1 to 2. It turns meals into person-years of protection.

rows.label: Food bought for the programme, 2025

source.title: World Central Kitchen, Inc. and Affiliate: consolidated financial statements, December 31, 2025 and 2024 (Grant Thornton, audited)
source.page: p. 8, consolidated statement of functional expenses, 2025, column Emergency Relief Programs

rows.explainer: The food line of the programme's functional expenses: what the ingredients and purchased meals cost.

rows.label: Food's share of programme spending
rows.explainer: The food bill over programme spending: about 71%. Each branch's food is its spending times this share, so all the food valued adds up to the food bill. The meals' value to the people eating them is the food's cost at normal prices, not the far higher prices in Gaza's markets during the blockade (which would value it many times higher) nor the full delivered cost (which would count cooking and logistics as value). The split by place is not published, so every branch takes the average share.

rows.label: Gaza, 2025: deaths from causes other than violence, per person-year, without the meals

source.title: RNZ / Reuters, 'Gaza deaths in war's first 15 months higher than reported, study says' (20 February 2026), on Spagat et al., The Lancet Global Health
source.quote: There were an estimated 16,300 non-violent deaths during the first 15 months of the war

rows.explainer: The first independent survey of deaths in Gaza (Spagat et al., Lancet Global Health, 2026; 2,000 households, interviews from 30 December 2024) estimated 16,300 non-violent deaths in the war's first 15 months: about 0.006 a person-year in some 2.1 million people. 2025 was worse: the March to May blockade and the famine the IPC confirmed for Gaza Governorate in August. Without the charity's meals (a large share of what its recipients ate) the rate would have been higher again. Our judgment for 2025, anchored on the survey's 0.006 for 2023-24 and the IPC's famine classification of August 2025: about 0.010, from 0.006 (the 2023-24 rate) to 0.025 (a third of the IPC famine threshold of 2 deaths per 10,000 a day, 0.073, which parts of Gaza may have reached). Violent deaths are left out: meals don't avert them.

rows.label: Death rate in Gaza's population before the war
rows.explainer: Palestine's crude death rate in 2022, the last year before the war (World Bank), so only the excess counts.

rows.label: Share of the excess deaths a daily hot meal averts among the people fed
rows.explainer: No study measures it. The excess deaths in Gaza in 2025 came from hunger, disease and a collapsed health system; a daily hot meal (about a third to a half of a person's food during the worst months) reaches the hunger part. Anchors: our relief models that restore health care or hand out goods credit 3-5% (American Red Cross 3%, Americares 5%); food in a famine acts on the main cause, so more: about 15%, from 5% to 35%.

rows.label: Years of the crisis each person in Gaza was fed
rows.explainer: The year's Gaza meals and bread over the people fed and the meals each gets a day: about a third of a year each.

rows.label: Deaths averted per person reached in Gaza (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Excess deaths over the time fed, times the share the meals avert.

rows.label: Share of the deaths averted that are of children under five
rows.explainer: Gaza's Ministry of Health counted about a third of its reported malnutrition deaths as children, but most non-violent excess deaths in the survey above were adults with chronic illness who lost care. Our judgment: 20%, from 10% to 35%, as our Americares emergency model.

rows.label: Of the deaths averted at five or older, share aged 5 to 14
rows.explainer: School-age children die least of hunger and disease in a famine once past five. About 8%, from 4% to 15% (our Americares and American Red Cross relief models use 10%).

rows.label: Of the deaths averted at 15 or older, share aged 15 to 49
rows.explainer: Most adult non-violent excess deaths are of the old and chronically ill (diabetes, kidney failure, cancer). About 30%, from 15% to 45%, as our Americares emergency model (the American Red Cross relief model uses 35%).

rows.label: Value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: The site's one value of a death, by age band, times your value of a life.

rows.label: Illness averted per person reached, in DALYs (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Not counted separately: the suffering of hunger is in the meals' consumption value below, and acute malnutrition that ends in death in the deaths. Counting wasting episodes as well would count hunger twice.

rows.label: US prices 2017 over 2025
rows.explainer: Puts the 2025 meals into 2017 prices, the PPP base.

rows.label: US prices 2017 over 2024
rows.explainer: Puts the 2024 consumption baselines into 2017 prices, the PPP base.

rows.label: Food delivered per person in Gaza in the year (US$)
rows.explainer: The Gaza branch's spending times food's share, over the people fed: about 140 dollars each (about 1.10 dollars a meal). Valued as consumption on top of the deaths averted: fewer than one person in a thousand fed is a death averted, so the consumption value is almost all to people who would have survived anyway (GiveWell likewise adds cash transfers' mortality effect to their consumption value).

rows.label: PPP conversion (2017 international $ per US $)
rows.explainer: Palestine's (World Bank).

rows.label: Consumption per person per year of the people fed in Gaza, without the meals (2017 international $)

source.title: UNCTAD, report on assistance to the Palestinian people (30 September 2025)
source.quote: GDP per capita dropped to $161

rows.explainer: In 2025 most of Gaza's food came from aid. Gaza's GDP per person fell to 161 dollars in 2024 (UNCTAD, constant 2015 dollars), from roughly 1,200 dollars in 2022 (the same report puts 2024's economy at 13.3% of 2022's, with a similar population); 2025 was no better; what people consumed was that plus the aid other agencies brought in, valued at normal prices. About 600 international dollars a year (1.6 a day), from 300 to 1,200. With the meals' value this sets the log gain, the model's largest driver.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per person in Gaza
rows.formula: years_exposed * ln(1 + value_delivered_per_person * cpi_2017_vs_2025 * ppp_factor / (baseline_consumption * years_exposed))
rows.explainer: The food on the site's one log-income scale over the time it was eaten: the meals raise consumption during the third of a year each person is fed (years_exposed), so the gain is years_exposed × ln(1 + food ÷ the consumption of that period).

rows.label: Crises in poorer countries: meals per person reached
rows.explainer: Responses there run from days (Hurricane Melissa, the Myanmar earthquake) to the whole year (Haiti's kitchens for displaced families and its school meals, front-line Ukraine). About 40, from 15 to 100.

rows.label: Crises in poorer countries: people reached
Crises in poorer countries: excess deaths per person-year among the people fed
rows.explainer: Haiti's gang crisis (over a million displaced, pockets of IPC phase 5 hunger in 2025), the Myanmar earthquake and front-line Ukraine raise deaths above normal much less than Gaza. About 0.003 a person-year above normal, from 0.0005 to 0.008 (our Americares emergency model: 0.012 against 0.0075, an excess of 0.0045).

rows.label: Crises in poorer countries: share of the excess deaths the meals avert
rows.explainer: Hunger is a smaller part of the excess there than in Gaza. About 5%, from 1% to 12%, as our Americares emergency model.

rows.label: Crises in poorer countries: deaths averted (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Person-years fed times the excess rate and the share averted, each death valued as in Gaza (the same mix of ages: hunger and disease deaths in a crisis).

rows.label: Weight: the Caribbean and Central America
Weight: East Asia and the Pacific (Myanmar as stand-in)
Weight: Ukraine and other middle-income places (Ukraine as stand-in)
rows.explainer: Ukraine, Mexico, Argentina, South Asia and Africa, valued at Ukraine's consumption.

rows.label: Jamaica's share of the Caribbean spending

source.title: World Central Kitchen: 'Community in Action', WCK in 2025
source.quote: hundreds of air deliveries of meals

rows.explainer: Hurricane Melissa hit Jamaica on 28 October 2025; the charity flew in hundreds of air deliveries and worked with dozens of restaurants there (its 2025 review) for the last two months of the year, while Haiti's kitchens ran all year (663 staff and contractors in the region, mostly Haitian). No split is published: about 30%, from 10% to 50%; the rest at Haiti's consumption.

rows.label: Affected households' consumption as a share of their country's survey mean
rows.explainer: As our American Red Cross relief and Americares emergency models (World Bank PIP anchors there): disaster-affected households are poorer than average and lost income.

rows.label: Myanmar: household consumption as a share of GDP
rows.explainer: The World Bank has no consumption series for Myanmar; neighbouring Bangladesh's households consume 70% of GDP (NE.CON.PRVT.ZS, 2024), as our American Red Cross relief and Americares emergency models.

rows.label: Jamaica: household consumption as a share of GDP
rows.explainer: The World Bank has no consumption series for Jamaica for 2019-24; Caribbean economies' households consume about 70-85% of GDP (Haiti far more, on remittances). About 75%, from 65% to 85%.

rows.label: Haiti: consumption of the people fed (2017 international $)
Jamaica: consumption of the people fed (2017 international $)
Ukraine: consumption of the people fed (2017 international $)
Myanmar: consumption of the people fed (2017 international $)
Crises in poorer countries: food per meal (US$, 2025)
rows.explainer: The branch's spending times food's share, over its meals.

rows.label: Crises in poorer countries: years each person was fed
rows.explainer: Meals per person over meals a day, in years: the period the food's gain is spread over.

rows.label: Haiti: ln(consumption) gain per person
rows.formula: lm_years_fed * ln(1 + lm_meals_per_person * lm_value_per_meal * cpi_2017_vs_2025 * @haiti.ppp_factor_2017 / (baseline_haiti * lm_years_fed))

rows.label: Jamaica: ln(consumption) gain per person
rows.formula: lm_years_fed * ln(1 + lm_meals_per_person * lm_value_per_meal * cpi_2017_vs_2025 * @jamaica.ppp_factor_2017 / (baseline_jamaica * lm_years_fed))

rows.label: Ukraine: ln(consumption) gain per person
rows.formula: lm_years_fed * ln(1 + lm_meals_per_person * lm_value_per_meal * cpi_2017_vs_2025 * @ukraine.ppp_factor_2017 / (baseline_ukraine * lm_years_fed))

rows.label: Myanmar: ln(consumption) gain per person
rows.formula: lm_years_fed * ln(1 + lm_meals_per_person * lm_value_per_meal * cpi_2017_vs_2025 * @myanmar.ppp_factor_2017 / (baseline_myanmar * lm_years_fed))

rows.label: Crises in poorer countries: ln(consumption) gain per person
rows.formula: w_cac * ((1 - jam_share_of_cac) * ln_gain_haiti + jam_share_of_cac * ln_gain_jamaica) + w_ukr * ln_gain_ukraine + w_mmr * ln_gain_myanmar
rows.explainer: The places' gains weighted by their spending.

rows.label: Rich-country disasters: meals per person reached
rows.explainer: US and European responses run days to a few weeks per place (the Los Angeles fires, the Texas floods); people come for a few meals. About 12, from 4 to 30.

rows.label: Rich-country disasters: people reached
Rich-country disasters: value of a meal (US$, 2025)
rows.explainer: The branch's spending times food's share, over its meals (restaurant and food-truck meals at US prices).

rows.label: Rich-country disasters: years each person was fed
rows.explainer: Meals per person over meals a day, in years.

rows.label: Rich-country disasters: consumption of the people fed over the US average
rows.explainer: Disasters in the US and Spain hit the poor and the well-off alike (the Los Angeles fires burned rich and middle-class neighbourhoods; Hurricane Helene's mountain towns are poorer than average). About 70%, from 45% (the US lowest fifth's share, @united_states.ce_lowest_quintile_vs_all_2024) to 100%. Spain and Italy are valued at US consumption too: they are under a tenth of the spending and of this branch's small value.

rows.label: Rich-country disasters: consumption of the people fed (2017 US$)
Rich-country disasters: ln(consumption) gain per person
rows.formula: hi_years_fed * ln(1 + hi_meals_per_person * hi_value_per_meal * cpi_2017_vs_2025 / (hi_baseline * hi_years_fed))
rows.explainer: No deaths are counted here: US and European disaster deaths come from the event itself, heat, cold or lost medical care, not hunger, and stores and other relief reopen within days; the meals' value is consumption.

rows.label: Gaza: evidence adjustment (internal and external validity), a multiplier
rows.explainer: How far to trust the meal count and the chain's inputs in this setting: the count is the charity's own and unaudited (the accounts say 179 million meals, its review 130 million). Looting and diversion are in delivery below, and that no study measures the meals' effect is the missing-data step's, not this one's. About 0.85, from 0.6 to 1, between our relief models (American Red Cross 0.95, Americares 0.8).

rows.label: Gaza: share of the meals other agencies wouldn't have delivered
rows.explainer: What limited food in Gaza in 2025 was access (crossings, truck numbers, the March-May blockade), not money: WFP and others had food waiting at the borders, so part of the food the charity brought in used crossing capacity others could have used. Against that, it cooked (fuel and kitchens were scarce), ran its own corridors (Jordan, Cyprus by sea) and bought some food locally. We found no count of its trucks against all food trucks into Gaza in 2025 (the UN2720 dashboard covers only UN-mechanism cargo and its figures are disputed). Anchored on our relief models' counterfactuals (Americares 0.5, American Red Cross 0.6, Doctors Without Borders relief 0.72), lowered for the crossing constraint: about half, from 25% to 80%.

rows.label: Crises in poorer countries: evidence adjustment, a multiplier
rows.explainer: As in Gaza: the charity's own, unaudited counts. About 0.85, from 0.6 to 1, between our relief models (American Red Cross 0.95, Americares 0.8).

rows.label: Crises in poorer countries: share of the meals others wouldn't have delivered
rows.explainer: In Haiti few others cook for the families displaced into Port-au-Prince's sites (a judgment: we found no cluster count of hot-meal providers); in Jamaica, Myanmar and Ukraine governments, WFP and others also fed people. About 60%, from 35% to 85%, as our American Red Cross relief model.

rows.label: Rich-country disasters: evidence adjustment, a multiplier
rows.explainer: The meal counts and their value at local prices are straightforward here. About 0.9, from 0.7 to 1.

rows.label: Rich-country disasters: share of the meals others wouldn't have provided
rows.explainer: After US disasters the Red Cross, the Salvation Army, churches, FEMA, disaster food stamps and reopening shops feed most people within days; the charity's meals mostly fill the first days and gaps. About 35%, from 15% to 60%.

rows.label: This charity's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: The charity pays for the food, the kitchens and the local partners' cooking (subcontractors), so most resources are its own. Others' are its 4,883 volunteers (Form 990 Part I, line 6; at the US value of a volunteer hour, 36 dollars, and some tens of hours each, a few million dollars, about 1-2% of spending), UN and Jordanian convoys and logistics it uses in Gaza, and restaurant partners' own capacity. About 90%, from 75% to 100%.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Delivery adjustment (meals reaching the people counted)
rows.explainer: Meals counted but not eaten by the people they were meant for: convoys looted in Gaza (the charity's own warehouse and trucks were hit, and it paused for a time), spoilage, double counting across partner kitchens. About 90%, from 75% to 100%.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: The charity raises its own money from the public (434 million dollars of gifts in 2025) and gets almost no government money, so a gift doesn't replace a government's; it ended the year with more unspent money (see the wait below). About 1, from 0.9 to 1.05.

rows.label: Income for local cooks, restaurants and farmers, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: The charity pays local restaurants, cooks and suppliers (29.4 million dollars of subcontractors, much of the food bought in the region): in Gaza and Haiti wages for people who had none. Their cost is in the model and the meals' value too, but the earnings above what the workers would otherwise get are not. About +5%, from 0 to +12%.

rows.label: Harms, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Crowds and danger at distribution points, and the risk to staff (seven were killed in an air strike in April 2024); relief that undercuts local food sellers where markets work. (Money held in reserve is in the wait discount.) About -5%, from -12% to 0.

rows.label: Hot meals over dry rations: time, fuel and dignity, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: A cooked meal saves fuel (scarce in Gaza: people burned furniture and plastic) and time, and people value being cooked for; the consumption value counts only the food. About +5%, from 0 to +15%.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: The three side effects above, summed.
